title: Everything You Own Owns a Piece of You, Too
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article extends a familiar observation about material possessions -- that they demand time, attention, and maintenance in proportion to their value -- into a lens on leadership roles. Taking on a new position, the author argues, works the same way: it 'owns' a piece of the leader's time, energy, and creativity, much like a house or a boat does. Rather than arguing against ownership or big commitments, the piece counsels readers to weigh that cost honestly before making a purchase or accepting a role. It closes with a memorable framing: we pay 'rent' in time and worry for everything valuable we own.
points: Meaningful possessions require ongoing time, attention, and resources proportional to their value.
Taking on a leadership role works the same way -- it demands and 'owns' a real share of a person's time and energy.
The point isn't to avoid big commitments, but to honestly weigh the ongoing cost before making them.
The article frames this cost as 'rent' paid in time and worry for anything genuinely valuable.
quotes: As they accumulate more material possessions, people typically come to a realization that perhaps should have been clear much earlier.
We don’t own anything of true value that doesn’t require our time, attention, maintenance, and resources.
When we agree to the responsibilities and commitments required in an elevated position, we invariably “own” the role as if it were a tangible thing.
It takes an enormous amount of time, energy, and creativity to excel at leading others.
Metaphorically speaking, we pay rent in time and worry for the most valuable things we own.
